idiom_name: std::function command registry keyed by step id + one central decision function
implementation_notes: The classic structure collapses into standard-library pieces: commands are std::function objects (or small classes with a virtual execute) kept in a std::map keyed by step or event id, and the central decision is an ordinary function Step next(Step, Event, const Session&) whose result names the next step; std::variant or std::optional carries the decision so the caller must handle every outcome. This registry form is the default when the toolchain is C++11 or newer and the flow is table-like. Hand-written command classes are still justified when commands carry real state or are registered by plugins, and the compile-time state machine alternative (see the variant) wins when guards, entry/exit actions and hierarchy matter more than the flexibility of a runtime map.
pitfalls: std::function allocates when the captured state exceeds its small buffer, and a registry copied per request copies every closure: keep the registry static/const and pass the session by reference.
Lambdas that capture references into a session outliving the request dangle; capture by value or (better) take the session as a parameter.
A registry keyed by std::string hides typos until runtime and the compiler cannot check the keys; key by an enum or expose the ids as named constants and test the decision table.

variants.name: Boost.MSM transition table (compile-time statechart)
variants.idiom_name: Boost.MSM Row/transition_table over a front-end state machine
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.MSM declares the flow as data checked at compile time: a transition_table of Row<State, Event, NextState, Action, Guard> entries inside an msm::front::state_machine_def, which the back-end state_machine processes events against. The Application Controller becomes the flow machine itself - events come from the UI, actions invoke the commands, guards decide conditional transitions, and illegal transitions do not compile. Choose it when guards, entry/exit actions and hierarchical states are worth the metaprogramming and the Boost dependency; for small flows the std::function registry stays the cheaper default.
pitfalls: Guards that return non-bool or touch state outside the machine make the compile-time checks cosmetic; keep them as pure predicates over the event and the machine's own data.
Error handling is a separate table: without an explicit no_transition handler, an unhandled event is swallowed silently.
